name: Space Harbour
description: There are $$$n$$$ points numbered $$$1$$$ to $$$n$$$ on a straight line. Initially, there are $$$m$$$ harbours. The $$$i$$$-th harbour is at point $$$X_i$$$ and has a value $$$V_i$$$. It is guaranteed that there are harbours at the points $$$1$$$ and $$$n$$$. There is exactly one ship on each of the $$$n$$$ points. The cost of moving a ship from its current location to the next harbour is the product of the value of the nearest harbour to its left and the distance from the nearest harbour to its right. Specifically, if a ship is already at a harbour, the cost of moving it to the next harbour is $$$0$$$. Additionally, there are $$$q$$$ queries, each of which is either of the following $$$2$$$ types: $$$1$$$ $$$x$$$ $$$v$$$ — Add a harbour at point $$$x$$$ with value $$$v$$$. It is guaranteed that before adding the harbour, there is no harbour at point $$$x$$$. $$$2$$$ $$$l$$$ $$$r$$$ — Print the sum of the cost of moving all ships at points from $$$l$$$ to $$$r$$$ to their next harbours. Note that you just need to calculate the cost of moving the ships but not actually move them.
input_specification: The first line contains three integers $$$n$$$, $$$m$$$, and $$$q$$$ ($$$2 \le m \le n \le 3 \cdot 10^5$$$, $$$1 \le q \le 3 \cdot 10^5$$$) — the number of points, harbours, and queries, respectively. The second line contains $$$m$$$ distinct integers $$$X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_m(1 \le X_i \le n)$$$ — the position at which the $$$i$$$-th harbour is located. The third line contains $$$m$$$ integers $$$V_1, V_2, \ldots, V_m(1 \le V_i \le 10^7)$$$ — the value of the $$$i$$$-th harbour. Each of the next $$$q$$$ lines contains three integers. The first integer is $$$t$$$ ($$$1\le t \le 2$$$) — type of query. If $$$t=1$$$, then the next two integers are $$$x$$$ and $$$v$$$ ($$$2 \le x \le n - 1$$$, $$$1 \le v \le 10^7$$$) — first-type query. If $$$t=2$$$, then the next two integers are $$$l$$$ and $$$r$$$ ($$$1 \le l \le r \le n$$$) — second-type query. It is guaranteed that there is at least one second-type query.
output_specification: For every second-type query, print one integer in a new line — answer to this query.
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1924B — Space Harbour [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
